test.topicName: Web APIs: requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback, IntersectionObserver, MutationObserver

questions.question: What is the primary behavioral difference between requestAnimationFrame(callback) and setTimeout(callback, 16) when used to drive a 60fps animation?
options: A) requestAnimationFrame runs the callback immediately before the browser's next repaint, is synced to the display's actual refresh rate, and is automatically paused in background/hidden tabs; setTimeout is a fixed timer unrelated to paint timing and historically keeps firing (often throttled to ~1s) in background tabs
B) They are functionally identical; requestAnimationFrame is just syntactic sugar for setTimeout(fn, 16)
C) setTimeout guarantees frame-perfect timing while requestAnimationFrame is best-effort and can be delayed indefinitely
D) requestAnimationFrame can only be used inside Web Workers, while setTimeout can only be used on the main thread
questions.correctAnswer: A) requestAnimationFrame runs the callback immediately before the browser's next repaint, is synced to the display's actual refresh rate, and is automatically paused in background/hidden tabs; setTimeout is a fixed timer unrelated to paint timing and historically keeps firing (often throttled to ~1s) in background tabs
questions.explanation: rAF callbacks are scheduled by the browser to run right before the next repaint, so they naturally adapt to 60Hz/90Hz/120Hz displays and pause when the tab is backgrounded (saving CPU/battery). setTimeout(fn, 16) is just a best-effort delay unrelated to the rendering pipeline — it can fire mid-frame, drift over time, and does not pause the same way, making it a poor primitive for smooth animation.

questions.question: You need to lazy-load images as they scroll into the viewport, without causing layout thrashing from repeated getBoundingClientRect() calls in a scroll handler. Which API is purpose-built for this?
options: A) A throttled `scroll` event listener calling `getBoundingClientRect()`
questions.explanation: IntersectionObserver asynchronously observes intersection changes between a target element and an ancestor/viewport off the main thread's synchronous layout path, avoiding the forced synchronous layout ('layout thrashing') that repeated getBoundingClientRect() calls inside scroll handlers cause.

questions.question: Inside a requestIdleCallback callback, what does `deadline.timeRemaining()` represent, and what is the significance of `deadline.didTimeout`?
options: A) `timeRemaining()` returns total idle time available for the rest of the page's lifetime; `didTimeout` indicates the browser crashed

B) `timeRemaining()` returns the milliseconds left in the current idle period (bounded, historically up to ~50ms); `didTimeout` is true when the callback was forced to run because its `timeout` option elapsed before an idle period occurred, even if the browser wasn't actually idle
C) `timeRemaining()` is a boolean; `didTimeout` returns the elapsed idle time in ms
D) Both properties are only meaningful when the callback is invoked from a Web Worker
questions.correctAnswer: B) `timeRemaining()` returns the milliseconds left in the current idle period (bounded, historically up to ~50ms); `didTimeout` is true when the callback was forced to run because its `timeout` option elapsed before an idle period occurred, even if the browser wasn't actually idle
questions.explanation: requestIdleCallback gives work a time budget per idle period. `timeRemaining()` lets you check how much of that budget is left so you can yield before blocking the next frame. If you pass `{ timeout }` and the browser never becomes idle in time, the callback still fires with `didTimeout: true` so starved low-priority work eventually runs — but `timeRemaining()` may report 0 or a very small value in that case since there's no real idle slack.

questions.question: If a script synchronously performs 50 separate DOM mutations on observed nodes within the same task (e.g., inside one function call, no awaits), how does a MutationObserver deliver these changes to its callback?
options: A) The callback fires synchronously 50 times, once per mutation, interleaved with the mutating code
B) The 50 mutations are compressed into an array of MutationRecords and delivered in a single callback invocation, scheduled as a microtask after the current synchronous task completes
C) Only the first mutation is recorded; the rest are silently dropped
D) Delivery requires an explicit call to `observer.flush()` after each mutation
questions.correctAnswer: B) The 50 mutations are compressed into an array of MutationRecords and delivered in a single callback invocation, scheduled as a microtask after the current synchronous task completes
questions.explanation: MutationObserver is asynchronous and batches records. The spec queues a compound microtask that flushes all pending observers once the current task finishes running (and before the next macrotask/rendering step), delivering the entire batch of MutationRecords as one array to the callback rather than firing per-mutation. `takeRecords()` can be used to synchronously drain the queue early if needed.

questions.question: In 3-5 sentences, explain why requestAnimationFrame is preferred over setTimeout/setInterval for driving visual animations. Name at least two concrete distinctions.
questions.correctAnswer: requestAnimationFrame schedules its callback to run right before the browser's next repaint, so updates are synchronized with the actual paint cycle and adapt automatically to the display's refresh rate (60Hz, 90Hz, 120Hz, etc.), whereas setTimeout/setInterval fire on a fixed wall-clock timer that has no relationship to painting and can easily fall out of sync with frames (causing jank, dropped frames, or wasted work between paints). rAF also automatically throttles/pauses when the tab is backgrounded or the page isn't visible, saving CPU and battery, while setTimeout/setInterval keep running (historically clamped to ~1s in background tabs by browsers, but still an uncoordinated separate mechanism). Additionally, the browser can batch style/layout recalculation work optimally around rAF callbacks since it knows exactly when they run relative to the rendering pipeline.
questions.explanation: Key grading points: (1) sync with repaint/refresh rate vs fixed timer, (2) automatic pause/throttle in background tabs, (3) avoids jank from misaligned timers, (4) enables the browser to schedule rendering work efficiently.

questions.question: requestIdleCallback has inconsistent browser support (notably absent in Safari) and known reliability pitfalls even where it exists. (a) List at least two reasons you should avoid relying on it for anything user-facing or time-critical. (b) Briefly describe how you'd implement a cross-browser fallback or an alternative scheduling strategy.
questions.correctAnswer: (a) Reasons to avoid for critical work: idle periods are not guaranteed to occur at all under sustained CPU/scroll/animation load, so callbacks can be starved indefinitely even with a `timeout`; the per-callback time budget is small and browser-determined (not something you control precisely); behavior differs across browsers/versions and is entirely unsupported in Safari; and idle callbacks may be deprioritized or not fire consistently in background tabs. (b) Fallback approaches: feature-detect `window.requestIdleCallback` and polyfill with `setTimeout(fn, 1)` plus a shimmed `IdleDeadline` object whose `timeRemaining()` is estimated from `performance.now()` against a fixed frame budget (e.g., 50ms minus elapsed frame time); alternatively use `requestAnimationFrame`-driven time-slicing (chunk work and yield back to rAF each frame, similar to React's Scheduler) or the newer `scheduler.postTask()` API with priority hints where available, reserving genuinely non-critical work (e.g., analytics batching, prefetch, non-visible DOM cleanup) for idle callbacks only when they do fire.
questions.explanation: Looking for: recognition that idle time isn't guaranteed, Safari has no native support, and a concrete fallback (setTimeout shim, rAF time-slicing, or scheduler.postTask). Bonus for distinguishing 'nice to have' vs 'must happen' work.

questions.question: MutationObserver callbacks are delivered as microtasks. Explain: (1) how this affects ordering relative to synchronous DOM mutations, Promise microtasks, and macrotasks like setTimeout; and (2) a subtle re-entrancy bug that can occur if the observer's own callback mutates the DOM node it's observing, and how to guard against it.
questions.correctAnswer: (1) MutationObserver queues a mutation-record microtask that runs after the current synchronous script/task finishes but before the event loop proceeds to rendering or the next macrotask (setTimeout/setInterval/I/O callbacks). It is interleaved with other microtasks like Promise `.then()` callbacks according to microtask queue order — if a Promise microtask was already scheduled before the mutation observer's delivery was queued, it runs first, and vice versa; both drain completely before any macrotask or paint. (2) If the callback itself synchronously mutates the observed node (e.g., updates an attribute it's watching), that mutation generates new MutationRecords for the same observer, which get appended to the queue and can cause the callback to be invoked again within the same microtask checkpoint (the microtask queue keeps draining until empty) — potentially producing an infinite loop or runaway recursion that hangs the tab. The fix is to guard re-entrancy: call `observer.disconnect()` before making the mutation inside the callback, perform the change, then call `observer.observe(...)` again to resume watching; alternatively use a flag/semaphore to skip self-triggered mutations, or check `record.oldValue`/`attributeName` to distinguish the observer's own writes from external ones.
questions.explanation: Grading focus: correct microtask ordering (after current task, before macrotasks/rendering, interleaved with Promise microtasks per queue order), and the disconnect/reconnect (or guard flag) pattern to prevent self-triggered infinite loops.

Tests understanding that `root` must match the actual scrolling container (defaults to viewport otherwise) and that IntersectionObserver can re-fire while an element remains intersecting, requiring explicit in-flight guarding — a very common real-world infinite-scroll bug.

Tests recognition of two compounding real-world bugs: missing `cancelAnimationFrame` cleanup (classic leak on unmount) and an unstable effect dependency causing multiple concurrent rAF loops to stack up. The fix pattern (ref for latest callback + empty-deps effect + cleanup) is a standard senior-level React/rAF idiom.

Tests deep understanding of MutationObserver's queue-drain-until-empty delivery semantics and the classic re-entrancy footgun of mutating the exact attribute/subtree you're observing inside the callback. Expect either the disconnect/reconnect guard or a redesign separating observed vs. derived state as a valid fix.
